about: Single source of truth for the demo videos: every scene's visual, on-screen action and narration. generate_narration.py turns 'text' into one audio file per scene; build_shot_lists.py turns this file into shot-lists.md. Edit here, then re-run both.

videos.title: The 30-second spiel
videos.notes: Fully animated. No screen recording: the Remotion composition Spiel30 is the whole picture. Drop the five audio clips under it in order.

scenes.text: We're moving our HR data to Databricks. But the rollout only moves tables.
And tables arrive without their meaning. Ask the same table for headcount at the end of Q2, and you get 58,862. <break time="0.3s" /> Or 175,524. Depending on who writes the query.

scenes.graphic: Spiel30 (part 3: five attritions and a spreadsheet)
scenes.text: Attrition has five versions. And who can see whose salary? That lives in a spreadsheet.
So I built a thin layer on top. A semantic layer. Every HR metric, and every access rule, defined once. So dashboards, Power BI, and AI all give the same answer.

scenes.action: None. Hold on the question for two seconds of silence before the end.
scenes.text: How much time does your team spend reconciling numbers before a leadership review?

videos.title: The 2-minute proof
videos.notes: Graphics open and close it; the middle is one SQL editor tab. Before recording, open hr_people_analytics/metrics/checks/workforce_checks.sql against the 70,000-person data, with the first two statements changed to show the naive and metric view headcount for 2025-Q2. Run both once so the warehouse is warm, then clear the results.

scenes.text: Our Databricks rollout is moving HR's tables across. What it doesn't move is the definitions. What counts as headcount. What counts as attrition. Who's allowed to see salary. Today, each of those lives in somebody's query, or somebody's spreadsheet. <break time="0.4s" /> Let me show you what that means, in about a minute. This is Tema, a fictional company of 70,000 people. About our size.

scenes.action: SQL editor, workforce_checks.sql. Put the cursor in the naive query (SUM(headcount) FROM v_headcount_naive, 2025-Q2) and run it. Let the result 175,524 sit on screen.
scenes.text: Here's headcount at the end of the second quarter of 2025, straight from the migrated table. <break time="0.3s" /> 175,524. For a company of 70,000.

scenes.action: Select (highlight) the SUM(headcount) and GROUP BY in the naive query so the zoom lands on it.
scenes.text: That's what happens when someone adds up April, May, and June. A perfectly reasonable query. The wrong answer. And nothing warns you.

scenes.action: Click into the metric view query (MEASURE(headcount) FROM workforce_metrics, 2025-Q2) and run it. Hover over 58,862.
scenes.text: Same table, same question, through the semantic layer. <break time="0.3s" /> 58,862. The rule, headcount is the last month of the period, never a sum, lives in the definition. So nobody can get it wrong. Not in SQL, not in the dashboard, not in Power BI, and not in Genie.
Has a number like the first one ever reached a leadership deck here?
And headcount is the easy one. Attrition is where it costs money. Once Tema had one definition of attrition, it could finally see that regretted leavers cost about 190 million dollars a year.

That's the future state. One certified definition per metric, with a named owner. One access rule. And every tool, including AI, reading from it. The migration is the foundation. This is the part that makes HR trust it. <break time="0.4s" /> If this sounds familiar, let's find thirty minutes to see whether it would work here.

videos.title: The 5-minute walk-through
videos.notes: Three proofs, each opened by a SectionCard. Open these tabs first, in this order: (1) workforce_checks.sql as for the 2-minute video; (2) Genie: 'Tema raw (baseline)' and 'People Analytics Assistant' in two tabs; (3) governance/02_hrbp_access_activity.sql with step 0 already run so hrbp_a, hrbp_b and manager_m are set; (4) the Workforce Overview dashboard as a fallback. Rebuild the governance model the same day (HRBP scope uses today's date).

scenes.text: Quick context. We're rolling out Databricks, and the plan is to move our HR tables there. That's necessary, but it's only the first half. Three things don't move with the tables. What our numbers mean. What AI is allowed to answer. And who's allowed to see sensitive people data. <break time="0.4s" /> Today those live in individual queries, BI tool settings, and a coverage spreadsheet. So we reconcile numbers before reviews, we're nervous about pointing AI at HR data, and HR business partner access breaks at every reorg. I built a working version of the fix, on a fictional 70,000-person company called Tema. Three things, five minutes.

scenes.graphic: SectionCard 1 before the clip; LowerThird 'Tema is fictional' on the clip
scenes.action: SQL editor, workforce_checks.sql. Run the naive headcount (175,524), pause, then run the metric view headcount (58,862).
scenes.text: First, the numbers don't agree. Here's headcount at the end of the second quarter of 2025, from the migrated table. 175,524. <break time="0.3s" /> And here's the same table, same question, through the semantic layer. 58,862. Someone added up three months, and nothing stopped them.

scenes.action: Catalog Explorer: open workspace.tema_hr_semantic, scroll the list of metric views, then open workforce_metrics and show the measures with their comments.
scenes.text: Every metric now has one definition, with an owner. Headcount, hires, leavers, attrition, time to fill, pay, engagement. More than fifteen KPIs across five areas, all in one place.

And because attrition now means one thing, we can cost it. Tema lost 2,782 regretted leavers in the last twelve months. That's about 190 million dollars a year to replace them, at half a salary each. The AI team alone, which grew about sixfold, accounts for 503 of them. About 67 million dollars.

scenes.graphic: QuestionCard: 'If we had one attrition number we trusted, what's the first decision you'd use it for?'
scenes.text: If we had one attrition number we trusted, what's the first decision you'd use it for?

scenes.action: Genie, two tabs side by side (or record each tab and place them side by side in the editor). Ask both: 'How many people did we have at the end of Q2 2025?' Wait for both answers.
scenes.text: Second, AI gives confident, wrong answers. Here's the same question, asked of Genie on the raw tables, and of our People Analytics Assistant on the semantic layer. The raw one adds up the months. The assistant answers 58,862.

scenes.action: Ask both agents for one named employee's salary (pick the employee in advance). Let the assistant's refusal and its reason stay on screen.
scenes.text: Now ask both for one person's salary. The assistant declines, and says why. The raw one may not.

scenes.graphic: BenchmarkCard (fill in scores in src/data.ts, or skip this graphic)
scenes.text: Same AI, same data. The difference is the definitions and rules underneath. On a twenty-question benchmark, the agent on the semantic layer got far more right than the one on raw tables. AI is only as good as the definitions under it, and the semantic layer is what makes it safe to give HR an AI assistant.

scenes.action: 02_hrbp_access_activity.sql: run step 2 (act as hrbp_a), then the 'where can hrbp_a see sensitive data' query by division.
scenes.text: Third, access to sensitive data doesn't follow the org. Here I'm acting as an HR business partner who supports two leaders in different divisions. They see salary and birthdays for everyone in both leaders' whole orgs, and only names and titles for everyone else.

scenes.action: Run step 4 (act as manager_m) and the sample rows query.
scenes.text: Now I'm a people manager. I see my direct reports' birthdays. No salaries.

scenes.action: Run step 6: end one of hrbp_a's assignments, rebuild the scope, rerun the division query. Show the salary counts drop.
scenes.text: And when one of those HR business partner assignments ends, I rebuild, and that access is gone. No tickets. No grant changes.

It's one rule in Unity Catalog. An HR business partner sees sensitive data for the whole orgs of the leaders they currently support. It's computed from the reporting lines and dated assignments. It handles partners with several leaders, and leaders with several partners. It keeps executives out. And it applies the same way in SQL, dashboards, BI tools, and Genie. Reorgs fix themselves overnight.

So here's the gap. Today, tables arrive in Databricks, definitions live in people's heads, access lives in a spreadsheet, and AI is off limits. <break time="0.4s" /> The future state: every HR number certified once, and the same everywhere. Sensitive data governed by one auditable rule. Definitions changed only by reviewed pull request. And an AI assistant HR business partners can actually use.

It doesn't compete with the migration. It reuses the migrated tables, adds a thin layer on top, and gives the migration team a definition of done. The ask is a 90-day pilot on people analytics. An HR sponsor, a named HR data owner, and about a day a week from one data engineer. <break time="0.4s" /> Who else should see this?
